### Fly strains

Fly strains used in this study are listed in Key resources table. Flies were raised on standard cornmeal medium at 22–23˚C on 12 hr-day: 12-hr-night cycle. PDM-DN is targeted by using the Split-GAL4 combination: y-w-; R23E07-p65.AD; VT002081-GAL4.DBD (PDM-DN-GAL4). SEZ-DN1 is targeted by using R75C02-GAL4. Wild-type background for Split-GAL4 lines is y-w- flies with empty attP40 and attP2 landing sites (y-w-; attP40, attP2). Wild-type background for GAL4 lines is w- flies with empty attP2 landing site. For control experiments, we used w- flies as wild-type background crossed to the UAS-TNTE effector line.

### Histology

Larval CNS were dissected and fixed in 4% formaldehyde (NC9658705, Thermo Fisher Scientific, MA, USA) in PBS (P4417, MilliporeSigma, MO, USA) for 1 hr at room temperature. After 3 times 15 min washes in PBS + 1% Triton X-100 (9284, TX, MilliporeSigma, MO, USA), the tissues were blocked for 1 hr at room temperature with 3% normal goat serum (G9023, MilliporeSigma, MO, USA) in 1% PBS-TX. The tissues were incubated with primary antibodies overnight at 4 ˚C. After 4 times 20 min washes in 1% PBS-TX, the samples were incubated with secondary antibodies for 4 hr at room temperature. Tissues were washed 4 times for 20 min with 1% PBS-TX followed by a short wash with PBS. The CNS were mounted in Vectashield mounting medium (H1000, Vector Laboratories, CA, USA) on lysine-coated (P8920, MilliporeSigma, MO, USA) coverslips and kept at 4 ˚C until imaged. Imaging was performed by using either a Leica SP5 or a Leica SP8 confocal microscope (Leica Microsystems, Wetzlar, Germany). Image rendering was performed with Fiji (ImageJ, http://fiji.sc/). Background correction, brightness and contrast adjustments, 3D rendering and maximum projections were performed by using Fiji. Antibodies and dilutions used in this study are listed in Key resources table. In order to detect CsChrimson::mVenus, we used conventional GFP antibodies (RRID: AB_221568 or RRID: AB_221569, Thermo Fisher Scientific, MA, USA). For MCFO experiments, we used an antibody against HA-tag (RRID: AB_1549585, Cell Signaling Technology, MA, USA). To label the neuropil, we used a combination of anti-brp (RRID: AB_2314866, Development Studies Hybridoma Bank, IA, USA) and anti-synorf1 (RRID: AB_2313867, Development Studies Hybridoma Bank, IA, USA) antibodies.

### Loss-of-function screen using Split-GAL4 driver lines

Split-GAL4 lines were crossed to UAS-TNTG (RRID: BDSC_28838, Bloomington Drosophila Research Center). Prior to tracking, 3rd instar larvae were kept in 15% sucrose (S0389, MilliporeSigma, MO, USA) for 20 min. After a quick wash in distilled water, twenty larvae were gently placed on 4% agar (DF0812-07-1, Thermo Fisher Scientific, MA, USA) slabs in 245 mm x 245 mm square Petri dishes using a small paint brush. Four odor droplets of 8 µl of 15mM ethyl butyrate (19230, MilliporeSigma, MO, USA) diluted in paraffin oil (Sigma-Aldrich) were pipetted inside the lid of the Petri dish (Figure 1—Figure supplement 1). Shortly after the lid was closed on the Petri dish, larvae were tracked for 6 min using Multi Worm Tracker software (http://sourceforge.net/projects/mwt). Behavioral data were analyzed using custom-written MATLAB scripts (https://github.com/LabLouis/eLife2018_PDM-DN; copy archived at https://github.com/elifesciences-publications/eLife2018_PDM-DN). The odor gradient was numerically simulated by using the analytical solution of an idealized diffusion problem from four point-odor sources in an environment with absorbing boundary conditions. At any given position in the assay ($x,y,z$), the odor concentration $Cr,t$ was modeled as $\frac{\gamma}{4 \pi D r}. erfc(\frac{r}{\sqrt{4 D t}})$ where $erfc(x)$ is the error function defined as $\int_{0}^{x}e^{−s^{2}}ds$ and $r$ denotes the distance to the source with coordinate ($x_{s},y_{s},z_{s}$): $r=\sqrt{x-x_{s}^{2}+y-y_{s}^{2}+z-z_{s}^{2}}$. Since we were only interested in reconstructing the geometry of the gradient and not its absolute concentration, the value of the flux of odor from the source was set arbitrarily equal to 1. The diffusion constant of the odor was approximated to 0.025 cm2/min.

### Single larva tracking experiments

In these experiments, UAS-TNTE was used to silence neural activity (Tastekin et al., 2015). Single larva tracking was performed as it was described before (Gomez-Marin et al., 2011). Briefly, 3rd instar larvae were kept in 15% sucrose for 20 min prior to tracking. Outer surface of 96 well plate lids without condensation rings were covered with 25 ml of 3% agarose (Seakem-LE, Lonza, Basel, Switzerland). 5 µl of odor (100 µM ETB or 1 mM EtA) was placed in one of the condensation rings in the middle of the 96 well plate lid with condensation rings (same ring location was used for all trials). The lid with the odor droplet was inverted on the agarose slab. The distance between the top of the lid and the agarose layer was sufficient to prevent any contact between the larva and the odor source (Gomez-Marin and Louis, 2012). A single larva was placed on the agarose surface approximately three wells away from the odor source. The larva was gently oriented towards the odor source and subsequently tracked for 5 min. The odor gradient was quantified by using a FT-IR spectrometer (Tensor 27, Bruker, MA, USA) as described elsewhere (Tastekin et al., 2015). Behavioral data were acquired, analyzed and quantified by using custom written MATLAB scripts (Tastekin et al., 2015) (updated version available via https://github.com/LabLouis/eLife2018_PDM-DN; copy archived at https://github.com/elifesciences-publications/eLife2018_PDM-DN).

### Gain-of-function manipulations for freely behaving larvae

GAL4/Split-GAL4 driver lines were crossed to 20XUAS-IVS-CsChrimson::mVenus in attP2 landing site (Bloomington Drosophila Research Center, RRID: BDSC_55136). For the gain-of-function experiments with ChAT-RNAi, 20XUAS-IVS-CsChrimson::mVenus in attP18 landing site was used (Bloomington Drosophila Research Center, RRID: BDSC_55134). Flies were kept in complete darkness on food supplemented with 0.5 mM all trans-retinal (R2500, MilliporeSigma, MO, USA). For optogenetic stimulation experiments, we used a red LED with peak emission at 625 nm (PLS 0625–030 s, Mightex Systems, Toronto, Canada). Single larvae were placed on a 2.5% agarose slab and tracked for 5 min using a closed-loop tracker (Schulze et al., 2015). For most of the experiments, we applied eight light flashes that were 6 s long. Consecutive flashes were separated by 30 s of no stimulation. For longer activation of the PDM-DN neuron, we applied 6 flashes of 20 s interspersed by 30 s of no stimulation. For head cast/turn-triggered activation experiments (Figure 3—figure supplement 2G–H), head casts/turns were classified online as described before (Schulze et al., 2015) and light flashes were kept on as long as the larva remained in head casting/turning mode.

### Stochastic gain-of-function assay

To unilaterally express CsChrimson::mVenus in the PDM-DN neuron, R57C10-Flp2::PEST;+; 20XUAS(FRT.stop)Chrimson::mVenus attP2 was crossed to (PDM-DN-GAL4). Flp2::PEST is a low activity flippase that allowed us to produce unilateral patterns of stochastic expression of CsChrimson::mVenus on one side of the brain (Nern et al., 2015). The larvae were blindly screened for gain-of-function behavior in the closed-loop tracker before their nervous system was isolated and immunostained against CsChrimson::mVenus.

### Gain-of-function manipulations for restricted larvae

Larvae at the 3rd instar developmental stage were pinned down on a PDMS slab (Sylgard 184 Silicone Elastomer Kit, Dow Corning) using stainless steel pins (26002–10, Fine Science tools, Vancouver, Canada). The pins were placed at the anterior end of the animal between the mouth hooks and at the posterior end of the animal between the tail spiracles. The segmental contractions were tracked by visualizing the denticle bands on the ventral side of the larva. Videos were recorded at a resolution of 1280 × 720 pixels and a rate of 20 Hz by using a USB3.0 CMOS camera (Grasshopper 3–41 C6M-C, Point Grey, Richmond, Canada). The movements of the denticle bands were analyzed by using Fiji and custom-written scripts in MATLAB. For optogenetic stimulations, we used a red LED with peak emission at 625 nm (PLS 0625–030 s, Mightex Systems, Toronto, Canada). We applied 6 s long flashes interspaced by 20 s. The camera and the LED were triggered with a NI-DAQ (NI USB-6525, National Instruments, TX, USA) and a custom written LabVIEW software (LabVIEW, National Instruments, TX, USA).

### Analysis of motor neuron activity and fictive locomotion

GAL4/Split-GAL4 lines were crossed to 20XUAS-IVS-CsChrimson.mVenus attP18; CG9887-LexA su(Hw)attP8; 12XlexAop2-IVS-GCaMP6f-p10 su(Hw)attP5 (gift from Stefan Pulver). CG9887-LexA (gift from Julie Simpson) targets GCaMP6f expression to glutamatergic neurons including all motor neurons. The central nervous system (CNS) of larvae at the 3rd instar developmental state were dissected in cold saline composed of 135 mM NaCl (S7653, MilliporeSigma, MO, USA), 5 mM KCl (P9571, MilliporeSigma, MO, USA), 2 mM CaCl2 (21115, MilliporeSigma, MO, USA), 4 mM MgCl2 (P2670, MilliporeSigma, MO, USA), 5 mM TES (T1375, MilliporeSigma, MO, USA) and 36 mM sucrose (S0389, MilliporeSigma, MO, USA). Isolated CNS were mounted on lysine-coated coverslips and covered with the saline solution. Imaging of motor neuron activity was performed with a Leica SP5 upright microscope using a 25X water immersion objective (NA. 95, 15506374, Leica Microsystems, Wetzlar, Germany) or 20X multi-immersion objective with a correction collar (NA 0.75, 15506343, Leica Microsystems, Wetzlar, Germany). Optogenetic activation of PDM-DN or SEZ-DN1 was performed by using a red LED with peak emission at 625 nm (PLS 0625–030 s, Mightex Systems, Toronto, Canada). The microscope and the LED were triggered with NIDAQs (NI USB-6229 and NI USB-6009, National Instruments, TX, USA) using custom written MATLAB scripts. Very low powers of Argon laser (488 nm) were used to excite GCaMP6f while avoiding the activation of CsChrimson at this wavelength. In the absence of 625 nm LED stimulus, waves of motor-neuron activity were observed (Figures 5 and 6) suggesting that the Argon laser did not interfere with CsChrimson activation. Recordings were performed at 4–5 Hz. The imaging data were analyzed using Fiji and custom written MATLAB scripts (https://github.com/LabLouis/eLife2018_PDM-DN; copy archived at https://github.com/elifesciences-publications/eLife2018_PDM-DN). Changes in the fluorescence signal were quantified as follows: region of interests (ROIs) were chosen for each segment on both sides of the VNC (see illustration in Figure 4G). The mean pixel intensity was calculated for each ROI. Baseline fluorescence intensity Fo was calculated as mean pixel intensity of the given ROI over the whole time series. For each time frame Fi, signals are computed as the relative change in fluorescence intensity from the baseline: ΔF/F= (Fi-F0)/F0 (Jia et al., 2011). The ΔF/F signal was filtered using Savitzky-Golay filtering with third order polynomial (frame length: 15).

### Imaging SEZ-DN1 activity in response to PDM-DN activation

Imaging experiments were performed with the following cross: 75C02-LexA/Cyo-Dfd::YFP; 13xLexAop2-IVS-GCaMP6f-p10 50.693 in VK00005, 20xUAS-CsChrimson-mCherry-trafficked in su(Hw)attp1 was crossed to PDM-DN-GAL4. The CNS of larvae at the 3rd instar developmental stage were dissected in cold saline (identical to the saline used in motor neuron imaging) and placed dorsal side down on a lysine-coated coverslip. We used an Ultima II two-photon scanning microscope (Bruker, MA, USA) and a Vision II laser (Coherent, CA, USA). For imaging we used two-photon excitation wavelength of 920 nm with the power at the sample never exceeding 10 mW. CsChrimson was activated with a LED (M590L3-C1, Thorlabs, NJ, USA) with peak wavelength at 590 nm and a 605/55 bandpass filter. To feed the CsChrimson excitation light into the light path, we used a custom dichroic dichroic (zt488-568, Chroma, VT, USA). The power of the LED from the objective was ~30 µW/mm2. Optogenetic activation stimuli were delivered in 30 Hz pulse trains (2 ms on, 31 ms off) lasting for 1 s. For trial the neuron was observed for approximately 20 s. Each trial was repeated 5 times. Functional imaging was analyzed by using custom written Python scripts (https://github.com/LabLouis/eLife2018_PDM-DN; copy archived at https://github.com/elifesciences-publications/eLife2018_PDM-DN). A ROI was chosen to contain only the axonal branching of the neuron of interest (Figure 6E). The signal was calculated as described previously (Jia et al., 2011). No noise filtering was applied. For each time frame Fi, signals were computed as the relative change in fluorescence intensity from the baseline: ΔF/F= (Fi-F0)/F0. Baseline fluorescence F0 was defined as the mean pixel intensity of a 2 s time window preceding the optogenetic stimulus.

### EM reconstruction using CATMAID

EM reconstruction of neurons and annotations of synapses were performed as described previously (Ohyama et al., 2015) using web-based software CATMAID (Saalfeld et al., 2009). An iterative reconstruction method was applied to reconstruct and annotate pre- and post-synaptic partners (Ohyama et al., 2015; Schneider-Mizell et al., 2016).

### Statistical analysis

Normality was tested using Lilliefors test. If distributed normally, data were analyzed with ANOVA test. When the Lilliefors test rejected normality, we used Wilcoxon ranksum test followed by Bonferroni correction. For paired data in Figure 3—figure supplement 3G, Figure 4H and Figure 6D, the Wilcoxon signed-rank test was used. For binomially distributed data, Clopper Pearson method was used to determine 95% confidence intervals. The cross correlation analysis was carried with the built-in corrcoef function of MATLAB_R2015b. To compare proportions in Figure 4F, we used a standard Z-test. More information about the statistical procedures can be found in the Transparency Report. The list of p-values corresponding to each statistical test of the study can be found in Supplementary file 1.

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.38740.028](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.38740.028)

In the interests of transparency, eLife includes the editorial decision letter and accompanying author responses. A lightly edited version of the letter sent to the authors after peer review is shown, indicating the most substantive concerns; minor comments are not usually included.

Thank you for submitting your article "Sensorimotor pathway controlling stopping behavior during chemotaxis in the Drosophila melanogaster larva" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by three peer reviewers, including Ronald L Calabrese as the Reviewing Editor and Reviewer #1, and the evaluation has been overseen by K VijayRaghavan as the Senior Editor. The following individual involved in review of your submission has agreed to reveal their identity: Jimena Berni (Reviewer #3).

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

Summary:

In this manuscript, the authors present a thorough analysis of circuit elements that mediate in olfactory guided stops and head casts associated with chemotaxis to an attractive odor in Drosophila larvae. In particular they concentrate on the role of a newly identified olfactory descending neuron, PDM-DN (bilateral pair), originating in the Lateral Horn region of the Brain Lobes and descending to the Ventral Nerve Cord. They use previous em reconstructions of the larval nervous system to identify upstream circuitry leading from olfactory receptor neurons, through specific olfactory Projection Neurons, through specific LH neurons to the PDM-DNs. They use the same reconstructions to further trace downstream circuitry focusing mainly on a path from the PDM-DNs onto the SubEsophageal Zone DN1 which then projects onto the previously characterized segmentally repeated (abdominal segments of the VNC) excitatory premotor interneurons A27h to which they connect in the posterior segments. The manuscript makes full use of current behavioral, intersectional genetics and optogenetic techniques available for circuit analyses of behavior in Drosophila and is guided by an em reconstruction of upstream and downstream synaptic targets. They perform critical necessity and sufficiency tests for the PDM-DNs and some downstream elements. The level of circuit analyses is impressive and it clearly shows that the PDN DNs play a critical role in the halts and head casts that accompany down-gradient runs in attractive chemotaxis. They also present a very convincing analysis of how PDM DN (and SEZ DN1) activation halts locomotory waves of contraction and fictive locomotory activity recorded with Ca indicator in the posterior abdominal segments of the VNC. The work is truly elegant and pushes the technology available. The elegance of both the analysis and the circuitry uncovered for mediating down-gradient run associated halts and head casts will be of wide interest.

The writing is clear and the figures are well organized, and clear.

Essential revisions:

1) Fundamental for the interpretation of all the results presented in the paper is the demonstration that the PDM-DNs plays a role in chemotaxis and not in crawling itself. The authors should show that when there is no odor and PDM-DNs are blocked, the larvae behave as their parental genetic controls. The experiment in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 no odor, should be performed with the same number of animals (30) required to see a significant difference in the chemotaxis experiment. If the behavior is not as the controls, then the entire paper will have to be reinterpreted and rewritten.

2) The sufficiency and necessity tests performed and the associated analyses are very impressive, and the data are convincing; however, they do not show necessity for halts or for head casts. Rather, they show that the PDN DNs play a critical role in halts and head casts associated with down-gradient runs but are not essential for such halts and head casts. Similarly, the sufficiency tests do not present an absolute result indicating that activation of the neuron produces a halt. It is not important to claim necessity or sufficiency but rather to present the impressive circuit analysis. Trying to fit these neurons in the Kupfermann and Weiss box of a command neuron may be the problem. It is not necessary to call these neurons command neurons for this work to be important. The experiments show that the PDN DNs are critically involved in the halt phase of chemotaxis, and PDN DNs provide a nexus for further circuit analysis and dissection of the behavioral mechanisms. Please re-frame your claims so that they are more nuanced and reflect the actual complexity of the whole system.

3) A synthesizing diagram in the manuscript that can tie in all of the observations (anatomical, functional, and behavioral) is missing. Even just a cartoon schematic would go a long way in making this work more easily digestible by all readers, including non-experts. This schematic could also effectively raise clearly the outstanding information for further experiments to determine the circuit mechanisms whereby PDM-DN and its downstream partners control halting and head-casting behaviors. What are the take-home messages to neuroscientists interested in behavioral control? We encourage the authors to provide such a synthesis in the final, published manuscript.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on adult fly behavior.

claims.claim: Flying insects such as pheromone-seeking male moths and foraging adult flies respond to attractive olfactory cues by implementing upwind 'surges', and exiting the odor plume triggers searches through casting behavior.
claims.source: Flying insects such as pheromone-seeking male moths and foraging adult flies respond to attractive olfactory cues by implementing upwind 'surges'. Exiting the odor plume triggers searches through casting behavior (Murlis et al., 1992; Bhandawat et al., 2010; van Breugel and Dickinson, 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on insect flight behavior.

claims.claim: Drosophila larvae display robust orientation behavior in response to food odors.
claims.source: Drosophila larvae display robust orientation behavior in response to food odors (Cobb, 1999).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Larval chemotaxis results from coordinated transitions between four behavioral primitives: runs, stops, head casts, and turns.
claims.source: Larval chemotaxis results from coordinated transitions between four behavioral primitives: runs (forward motion by means of symmetrical peristaltic contractions), stops (cessation of peristaltic waves), head casts (lateral head sweeps) and turns (asymmetrical contractions of the body segments followed by straightening of the body) (Green et al., 1983; Gomez-Marin et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies that characterized larval behavior.

claims.claim: Larvae time the initiation of reorientation maneuvers based on the detection of negative sensory gradients.
claims.source: To accurately navigate attractive odor gradients, larvae implement two sensorimotor tasks: they time the initiation of reorientation maneuvers based on the detection of negative sensory gradients (Figure 1Ai)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1Ai and previous studies (Gomez-Marin and Louis, 2012).

claims.claim: Larvae direct turns toward the local odor gradient.
claims.source: and they direct turns toward the local odor gradient (Gomez-Marin and Louis, 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Acute activations of olfactory sensory neurons through optogenetics have established quantitative relationships between the activity of the peripheral olfactory system and the release of specific motor programs such as stops.
claims.source: Acute activations of olfactory sensory neurons (OSNs) through optogenetics have established quantitative relationships between the activity of the peripheral olfactory system and the release of specific motor programs such as stops prior to the initiation of reorientation maneuvers (Gepner et al., 2015; Hernandez-Nunez et al., 2015; Schulze et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous optogenetic studies.

claims.claim: Nonlinear aspects of the input-output response properties of larval OSNs are essential to explain how dynamic patterns of stimulus intensity evoke predictable and stereotypical sequences of behavioral control.
claims.source: Nonlinear aspects of the input-output response properties of the larval OSNs are essential to explain how dynamic patterns of stimulus intensity evoke predictable and stereotypical sequences of behavioral control (Schulze et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: The larval olfactory system comprises only 21 olfactory sensory neurons.
claims.source: The larval olfactory system is compact: it comprises only 21 olfactory sensory neurons (OSN) (Fishilevich et al., 2005; Kreher et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claims.claim: The axon terminals of OSNs synapse onto second-order projection neurons (PNs) in the antennal lobe.
claims.source: The axon terminals of OSNs synapse onto second-order projection neurons (PNs) in the antennal lobe (AL).
claims.evidence: This is a well-established anatomical fact about the larval olfactory system.

claims.claim: The anatomical organization of the larval antennal lobe has been characterized through a combination of light and electron microscopy.
claims.source: The anatomical organization of the larval AL has been characterized through a combination of light and electron microscopy (Ramaekers et al., 2005; Masuda-Nakagawa et al., 2009; Berck et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claims.claim: The axons of PNs project to two main neuropil centers in the larval brain lobes: the lateral horn and the mushroom body.
claims.source: The axons of the PNs project to two main neuropil centers in the larval brain lobes where further sensory processing takes place: the lateral horn (LH) and the mushroom body (MB).
claims.evidence: This is a well-established anatomical fact about the larval olfactory system.

claims.claim: The entire connectome of the larval mushroom body has been reconstructed using electron microscopy.
claims.source: The entire connectome of the larval MB has been reconstructed using electron microscopy (Eichler et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: In adult Drosophila, PN axons arising from the same glomerulus of the antennal lobe converge onto stereotyped and overlapping regions of the lateral horn.
claims.source: In the adult Drosophila, PN axons arising from the same glomerulus of the AL converge onto stereotyped and overlapping regions of the LH (Marin et al., 2002; Wong et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies in adult flies.

claims.claim: Distinct odors trigger calcium responses in specific regions of the lateral horn in a concentration-dependent manner.
claims.source: Distinct odors trigger calcium responses in specific regions of the LH in a way that is concentration-dependent (Strutz et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Pre-motor circuits located in the ventral nerve cord are responsible for generating patterns of rhythmic motor activities that create peristaltic motion through stereotyped sequences of muscle contractions.
claims.source: At the other end of the central nervous system of the larva, pre-motor circuits located in the ventral nerve cord (VNC) are responsible for generating patterns of rhythmic motor activities that create peristaltic motion through stereotyped sequences of muscle contractions (Inada et al., 2011; Berni et al., 2012; Kohsaka et al., 2012; Berni, 2015; Pulver et al., 2015; Fushiki et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on larval motor circuits.

claims.claim: Central pattern generating networks underlie the production of rhythmic motor output in the absence of sensory feedback or input from other brain regions.
claims.source: Central pattern generating (CPG) networks underlie the production of rhythmic motor output in the absence of sensory feedback or input from other brain regions (Marder and Calabrese, 1996; Katz, 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work on CPG networks.

claims.claim: Isolated larval central nervous systems are sufficient to produce segmentally-coordinated motor output, suggesting that CPGs underlying peristalsis are located in segmentally-organized network elements in the VNC.
claims.source: The observation that isolated larval central nervous systems (CNS) are sufficient to produce segmentally-coordinated motor output suggests that the CPGs underlying peristalsis are located in segmentally-organized network elements in the VNC (Fox et al., 2006; Inada et al., 2011; Berni et al., 2012; Berni, 2015; Lemon et al., 2015; Pulver et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on isolated CNS preparations.

claims.claim: Descending neural pathways create a bottleneck in sensorimotor transformations by creating an interface between circuits that carry out sensory processing in the brain lobes and those in charge of motor pattern generation in the VNC.
claims.source: Descending neural pathways create a bottleneck in sensorimotor transformations: they create an interface between the circuits that carry out sensory processing in the brain lobes and those in charge of motor pattern generation in the VNC.
claims.evidence: This is a conceptual statement about the role of descending neurons in sensorimotor control.

claims.claim: Descending neurons are often regarded as key elements of 'command' circuits that condition the release of naturally occurring motor programs.
claims.source: Descending neurons are often regarded as key elements of 'command' circuits that condition the release of naturally occurring motor programs (Kristan, 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work on command neurons.

claims.claim: In the leech, descending 'command' neurons with somas in the subesophageal zone integrate mechanosensory inputs to trigger segmental swim-initiating circuits in the VNC.
claims.source: The leech provides a prime example of descending 'command' neurons with somas in the subesophageal zone (SEZ) where mechanosensory inputs are integrated to trigger segmental swim-initiating circuits in the VNC (Brodfuehrer and Friesen, 1986).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work on leech descending neurons.

claims.claim: In adult Drosophila, activation of distinct descending neurons can elicit stereotypic behaviors such as backward walking and courtship song.
claims.source: In adult Drosophila, activation of distinct descending neurons can elicit stereotypic behaviors such as backward walking (Bidaye et al., 2014) and courtship song (von Philipsborn et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on adult fly descending neurons.

claims.claim: Most descending neurons in adult Drosophila produce a single behavioral output, while a minority trigger multiple behavioral outputs that are manifested either simultaneously or sequentially.
claims.source: Recently, a detailed analysis of a large collection of Split-Gal4 driver lines targeting distinct descending neuron populations has concluded that most descending neurons produce a single behavioral output, while a minority of descending neurons are sufficient to trigger multiple behavioral outputs that are manifested either simultaneously or sequentially (Cande et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work on adult fly descending neurons.

claims.claim: In the larva, descending inputs from the brain lobes and SEZ are necessary to regulate the speed and frequency of CPGs in charge of the actuation of forward runs, stop-turns, and backward runs.
claims.source: In the larva, descending inputs from the brain lobes (BL) and SEZ are necessary to regulate the speed and frequency of the CPGs in charge of the actuation of forward runs, stop-turns and backward runs (Berni et al., 2012; Pulver et al., 2015; Tastekin et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on larval descending neurons.

claims.claim: A loss-of-function screen was conducted on a large collection of Split-Gal4 driver lines to identify neurons in the larval brain involved in chemotaxis behavior.
claims.source: To identify neurons in the larval brain involved in chemotaxis behavior, we conducted a loss-of-function (LoF) screen on a large collection of Split-Gal4 driver lines (Li et al., 2014; Dionne et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claims.claim: Acute loss-of-function impairments were achieved by blocking synaptic transmission with tetanus toxin light chain.
claims.source: Acute LoF impairments were achieved by blocking synaptic transmission with tetanus toxin light chain (TNT) (Sweeney et al., 1995).
claims.evidence: This describes the method used to silence neurons in the screen.

claims.claim: The screen was based on a modified version of a high-throughput olfactory assay using the multi-worm tracker to track orientation behavior of multiple larvae simultaneously.
claims.source: The screen was based on a modified version of a high-throughput olfactory assay introduced in previous work (Tastekin et al., 2015). The spatio-temporal resolution of the loss-of-function characterization was enhanced by using the multi-worm tracker (MWT) (Swierczek et al., 2011), which allowed us to track orientation behavior of multiple larvae simultaneously in a single trial (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental setup used in the screen, with reference to Figure 1B.

claims.claim: The behavioral assay consisted of a large square dish coated with agar with four hanging droplets of an attractive odor in the lid.
claims.source: The assay consisted of a large square dish coated with agar. The lid of the dish was outfitted with four hanging droplets of an attractive odor (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental setup, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Each of the four odor sources created a gradient that acted like a spatial attractor on the behavior of single larvae.
claims.source: Each of the four odor sources created a gradient, which acted like a spatial attractor on the behavior of single larvae (Figure 1Biii and Figure 1Biv).
claims.evidence: This describes the behavioral effect of the odor sources, with reference to Figure 1Biii and 1Biv.

claims.claim: Twenty larvae were placed in the middle of the arena and tracked for 5 minutes.
claims.source: We placed 20 larvae in the middle of the arena and tracked their trajectories for 5 min (Figure 1Bi and Figure 1Bii).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claims.claim: The initial orientation of a larva was a key factor determining the source under which it resided.
claims.source: We observed empirically that the initial orientation of a larva was a key factor determining the source under which it resided (Figure 1Biii and Figure 1Biv).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1Biii and 1Biv.

claims.claim: Multiple sources were used to minimize interactions between individual larvae by distributing their accumulation across four regions of the plate.
claims.source: Multiple sources were used to minimize interactions between individual larvae by distributing their accumulation across four regions of the plate (Figure 1Biii and Figure 1Biv).
claims.evidence: This explains the rationale for using four odor sources in the assay.

claims.claim: Approximately 300 Split-Gal4 driver lines were screened, most of which labeled only a single neuron per brain hemisphere.
claims.source: We screened ~300 Split-Gal4 driver lines most of which labeled only a single neuron per brain hemisphere (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This describes the scope of the screen.

claims.claim: Silencing neurons labeled by eighteen different Split-Gal4 driver lines led to a statistically significant increase or decrease in chemotactic performances.
claims.source: Silencing neurons labeled by eighteen different Split-Gal4 driver lines led to a statistically significant increase or decrease in chemotactic performances (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the screen shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: A Split-Gal4 line was identified that specifically labels an olfactory descending neuron (PDM-DN) connecting the lateral horn region of the brain lobes to the ventral nerve cord.
claims.source: This approach permitted the identification of a Split-Gal4 line that specifically labels an olfactory descending neuron (PDM-DN) connecting the lateral horn region of the brain lobes to the ventral nerve cord (Figure 1C and Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is a key finding from the screen, shown in Figures 1C and 2A.

claims.claim: The loss-of-function phenotype associated with PDM-DN silencing demonstrated an overall reduction in the accuracy of chemotaxis manifested as a wider spread of individual trajectories around the odor sources.
claims.source: The LoF phenotype associated with the expression of TNT in PDM-DN (PDM-DN>TNT) demonstrated an overall reduction in the accuracy of chemotaxis manifested as a wider spread of individual trajectories around the odor sources (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This describes the behavioral phenotype observed upon PDM-DN silencing, shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: PDM-DN-silenced larvae remained further away from the odor source than their positive controls during the first three minutes of a trial.
claims.source: During the first three minutes of a trial, PDM-DN>TNT larvae (Figure 1E, magenta trace) remained further away from the source than their positive controls (Figure 1E, black trace).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the behavioral assay shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: While parental-control larvae stayed at an average distance of ~13 mm to the nearest source between 120 and 240 s, PDM-DN silenced larvae remained at a larger distance (~19 mm) during the same period.
claims.source: While parental-control larvae stayed at an average distance of ~13 mm to the nearest source between 120 and 240 s, PDM-DN silenced larva remained at a larger distance (~19 mm) during the same period of time.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the behavioral assay.

claims.claim: The loss-of-function defect of PDM-DN did not result from an overall decrease in locomotor speed.
claims.source: The LoF defect did not result from an overall decrease in locomotor speed (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A)
claims.evidence: This is a control result shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claims.claim: PDM-DN silencing resulted in a significant decrease in turn rate.
claims.source: but a significant decrease in turn rate (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the behavioral analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claims.claim: In spite of the significant turning defect, the ability of PDM-DN>TNT larvae to orient toward the odor gradient was sufficient to produce significant accumulation under the source compared to the no-odor control.
claims.source: In spite of this significant turning defect, the ability of PDM-DN >TNT larvae to orient toward the odor gradient was sufficient to produce significant accumulation under the source compared to the no-odor control (Figure 1Biv and E and F).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral data shown in Figures 1Biv, 1E, and 1F.

claims.claim: The PDM-DN neurons form a pair of bilaterally symmetrical cells in each brain lobe.
claims.source: The PDM-DN neurons form a pair of bilaterally symmetrical cells in each brain lobe (Figure 2Ai).
claims.evidence: This is an anatomical observation shown in Figure 2Ai.

claims.claim: Each PDM-DN sends its dendrite and axon contralateral to its cell body.
claims.source: By using the MultiColor FlpOut (MCFO) technique to reveal the anatomy of individual neurons (Nern et al., 2015), we showed that each PDM-DN sends its dendrite and axon contralateral to its cell body (Figure 2Aiv).
claims.evidence: This is an anatomical observation shown in Figure 2Aiv using the MCFO technique.

claims.claim: The soma of PDM-DN is located in the posterior-dorsal-medial region of the brain.
claims.source: The soma of PDM-DN is located in the posterior-dorsal-medial region of the brain (Figure 2Aii).
claims.evidence: This is an anatomical observation shown in Figure 2Aii.

claims.claim: PDM-DN has dendritic arborizations around the mushroom body peduncle and near the lateral horn region, suggesting that PDM-DN receives olfactory input.
claims.source: Closer inspection revealed that PDM-DN has dendritic arborizations around the mushroom body (MB) peduncle (the axonal bundle of Kenyon cells preceding the formation of the MB lobes) and near the lateral horn (LH) region, suggesting that PDM-DN receives olfactory input (Figure 2Aiii).
claims.evidence: This is an anatomical observation shown in Figure 2Aiii, with an inference about function.

claims.claim: The axon of PDM-DN extends to the VNC dorso-medially and targets three regions: the subesophageal zone, the thoracic neuromeres, and the first four abdominal neuromeres.
claims.source: The axon of PDM-DN extends to the VNC dorso-medially (Figure 2Ai, left inset) and targets three regions: the subesophageal zone (SEZ), the thoracic neuromeres and the first four abdominal neuromeres (Figure 2Ai).
claims.evidence: This is an anatomical observation shown in Figure 2Ai.

claims.claim: PDM-DN was identified in the EM stack based on the unequivocal resemblance of the candidate neuron reconstructed from EM and light microscopy.
claims.source: We identified PDM-DN in the EM stack based on the unequivocal resemblance of the candidate neuron reconstructed from the EM and light microscopy (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This describes the method used to identify PDM-DN in the EM data.

claims.claim: Ethyl butyrate predominantly activates two olfactory sensory neurons at moderate concentrations: Or42a and Or42b.
claims.source: This odor predominantly activates two olfactory sensory neurons (OSNs) at the moderate concentrations used in our LoF experiments: Or42a and Or42b (Kreher et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is a fact about odor-receptor interactions supported by a citation.

claims.claim: PDM-DN receives the strongest olfactory inputs from the Or42a and Or42b OSNs through the lateral horn region.
claims.source: We traced the pre-synaptic partners of PDM-DN all the way up to the sensory periphery and found that PDM-DN receives the strongest olfactory inputs from the Or42a and Or42b OSNs through the lateral horn region (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is a result from EM reconstruction shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The uniglomerular projection neurons downstream from the Or42a and Or42b OSNs directly innervate the local interneuron LH-LN1 in the lateral horn region.
claims.source: The uniglomerular projection neurons (PNs) downstream from the Or42a and Or42b OSNs directly innervate the local interneuron LH-LN1 in the lateral horn region (Figure 2B–C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is a result from EM reconstruction shown in Figures 2B-C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: LH-LN1 receives ipsilateral input from olfactory projection neurons and sends axonal projections that bilaterally synapse onto PDM-DN and onto a second local interneuron in the lateral horn region, LH-LN2.
claims.source: While LH-LN1 receives ipsilateral input from olfactory projection neurons, it sends axonal projections that bilaterally synapse onto PDM-DN and onto a second local interneuron in the lateral horn region, LH-LN2 (Figure 2B–C).
claims.evidence: This is a result from EM reconstruction shown in Figures 2B-C.

claims.claim: LH-LN2 gives bilateral inputs to PDM-DN.
claims.source: In addition, LH-LN2 gives bilateral inputs to PDM-DN (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is a result from EM reconstruction shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: The circuit motif encompassing LH-LN1, LH-LN2, and PDM-DN constitutes a feedforward motif downstream from the olfactory projection neurons.
claims.source: The circuit motif encompassing LH-LN1, LH-LN2 and PDM-DN constitute a feed-forward motif (Alon, 2006) downstream from the olfactory projection neurons.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the circuit connectivity with reference to a known circuit motif.

claims.claim: Silencing PDM-DN compromised the ability of larvae to accurately locate the nearest odor source and to stay under this position in a single-odor-source assay.
claims.source: Consistent with the results of group behavior tested in the four-odor-source assay (Figure 1D), a visual inspection of the trajectories of PDM-DN>TNT and its parental controls revealed that silencing the function of PDM-DN compromised the ability of larvae to accurately locate the nearest odor source and to stay under this position (Figure 3A–B).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the single-larva tracking assay shown in Figures 3A-B.

claims.claim: Both parental controls and PDM-DN>TNT larvae accumulate near the source after a transient phase (~30 s) during which larvae moved up the gradient.
claims.source: By quantifying the orientation behavior through the distance to the source, we observed that both parental controls and the PDM-DN>TNT larvae accumulate near the source after a transient phase (~30 s) during which larvae moved up the gradient.
claims.evidence: This is a result from the behavioral analysis.

claims.claim: The average distance to the source of PDM-DN silenced larvae gradually increased after ~120 s while it remained stationary for both parental controls during ~240 s.
claims.source: Unlike the results of the four-odor-source assay (Figure 1), the average distance to the source of the PDM-DN silenced larvae gradually increased after ~120 s (Figure 3C, magenta trace) while it remained stationary for both parental controls during ~240 s (Figure 3C, blue and black traces).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the behavioral analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Silencing PDM-DN did not significantly decrease the run speed of PDM-DN>TNT larvae compared to the slowest parental control.
claims.source: This difference is unlikely to be explained by an overall reduction in locomotor activity given that silencing PDM-DN did not significantly decrease the run speed of PDM-DN>TNT larvae compared to the slowest parental control (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and H).
claims.evidence: This is a control result shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and H.

claims.claim: Significant differences in run speeds were observed between the two parental controls, likely caused by genetic background.
claims.source: We nonetheless observed significant differences in the run speeds of the two parental controls — an effect likely caused by genetic background.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the data with an inference about the cause.

claims.claim: PDM-DN>TNT larvae turned less frequently than either parental control in a time window during the middle of the experiment (120-180 s).
claims.source: In agreement with the results of the four-odor-source assay (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), we found that PDM-DN>TNT larvae turned less frequently than either parental control (Figure 3D, left).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the behavioral analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: A difference in turn rates was only observed for down-gradient runs when turn rates were conditioned on the sensory experience of the larva.
claims.source: We then conditioned the turn-rate analysis on the sensory experience of the larva: turn rates were measured separately for up-gradient and down-gradient runs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C). A difference in turn rates was only observed for down-gradient runs.
claims.evidence: This is a result from the behavioral analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Silencing PDM-DN reduces the likelihood that larvae terminate runs associated with negative changes in odor concentration.
claims.source: Therefore, we conclude that silencing PDM-DN reduces the likelihood that larvae terminate runs associated with negative changes in odor concentration.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral data.

claims.claim: The likelihood of turning during the up-gradient phase of a run was unaffected by the loss-of-function manipulation of PDM-DN.
claims.source: By contrast, the likelihood of turning during the up-gradient phase of a run was unaffected by the LoF manipulation.
claims.evidence: This is a result from the behavioral analysis.

claims.claim: Silencing PDM-DN did not lead to a decrease in turn rate in the absence of odor gradients.
claims.source: In addition, silencing of PDM-DN did not lead to a decrease in turn rate in the absence of odor gradients, supporting the idea that the PDM-DN LoF phenotype is not due to an overall decrease in run-to-turn transitions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G and H).
claims.evidence: This is a control result shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G and H.

claims.claim: Larvae with silenced PDM-DN displayed no decrease in the accuracy of the orientation of their turns.
claims.source: Larvae with silenced PDM-DN displayed no decrease in the accuracy of the orientation of their turns.
claims.evidence: This is a result from the behavioral analysis.

claims.claim: One parental control showed a significant reduction in turning performances compared to PDM-DN>TNT and the other parental control.
claims.source: Interestingly the parental control (SS01994 x w-/-) showed a significant reduction in turning performances compared of PDM-DN>TNT and the other parental control (Figure 3D, right panel).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the behavioral analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: The decrease in reorientation performances of one parental control might be due to the higher locomotor speed displayed by this control, which might compromise the speed-accuracy tradeoff necessary to accurately sample and navigate odor space.
claims.source: This decrease in reorientation performances might be due to the higher locomotor speed displayed by this parental control (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), which might compromise the speed-accuracy tradeoff necessary to accurately sample and navigate odor space (Chittka et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral data with reference to a general principle.

claims.claim: Optogenetically-induced activation of PDM-DN produced a nearly deterministic switch from an ongoing run to a stop-turn.
claims.source: Optogenetically-induced activation of PDM-DN produced a nearly deterministic switch from an ongoing run to a stop-turn (Video 1).
claims.evidence: This is a result from optogenetic experiments shown in Video 1.

claims.claim: The switch from running to stopping upon PDM-DN activation was highly reproducible.
claims.source: The switch from running to stopping was highly reproducible (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This is a result from optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: A series of 8 consecutive light flashes produced eight transitions from a run to a stop-turn.
claims.source: A series of 8 consecutive light flashes produced eight transitions from a run (high-tail speed) to a stop-turn (low-tail speed) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This is a result from optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: Averaging the time course of tail-speed over 280 flashes yielded a stereotyped decrease in tail speed associated with the interruption of forward locomotion.
claims.source: Averaging the time course of the tail-speed over 280 flashes yielded a stereotyped decrease in tail speed associated with the interruption of forward locomotion (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This is a result from optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: The non-zero value of the average tail speed resulted from inter-trial variability in the timing of stops.
claims.source: The non-zero value of the average tail speed resulted from inter-trial variability in the timing of stops (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A.

claims.claim: Negative parental controls only showed a modest decrease in tail speed likely arising from startle responses.
claims.source: By contrast, negative parental controls only showed a modest decrease in tail speed that is likely to arise from startle responses.
claims.evidence: This is a result from control experiments with an inference about the cause.

claims.claim: The probability that wild-type controls stopped in response to light was nearly null and markedly lower than PDM-DN>CsChrimson larvae.
claims.source: The probability that wild-type controls stopped in response to light was nearly null and markedly lower than PDM-DN>CsChrimson larvae (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: This is a result from optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: In few cases where wild-type larvae stopped, the average duration of stopping behavior was shorter compared to PDM-DN activation.
claims.source: In few cases where wild-type larvae stopped, the average duration of stopping behavior was also shorter compared to the PDM-DN activation (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This is a result from optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: The probability of stopping was anti-correlated with tail speed in negative controls, but no dependence between stop probability and tail speed was found for PDM-DN>CsChrimson larvae.
claims.source: While we observed that the probability of stopping was anti-correlated with the tail speed in negative controls, no dependence between the stop probability and tail speed was found for PDM-DN>CsChrimson larvae, highlighting the deterministic nature of the optogenetic activation phenotype (Figure 3G).
claims.evidence: This is a result from optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 3G.

claims.claim: When subjected to a longer 20-s red-light flash, the majority of PDM-DN>CsChrimson larvae remained in stopping mode for ~3 s, but the average tail speed gradually increased throughout the duration of the flash.
claims.source: When subjected to a longer 20-s-red-light flash, the majority of PDM-DN>CsChrimson larvae remained in stopping mode for ~3 s, but the average tail speed gradually increased throughout the duration of the flash (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 4A, right panels).
claims.evidence: This is a result from optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 4A.

claims.claim: The gradual increase in tail speed during prolonged PDM-DN activation indicated a failure to sustain stopping behavior, suggesting adaptation of the PDM-DN neuron or circuit-level mechanisms that bypass stopping behavior over longer durations.
claims.source: This gradual increase in tail speed indicated a failure to sustain stopping behavior, thereby suggesting an adaptation of the PDM-DN neuron in response to persistent optogenetic activation or circuit-level mechanisms that bypass stopping behavior over longer durations (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A, right panels).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A.

claims.claim: Optogenetic activation of PDM-DN produced a delayed increase in average head-angle speed peaking at ~3 s into the light activation.
claims.source: Unlike the parental controls, the optogenetic activation of PDM-DN produced a delayed increase in the average head-angle speed peaking at ~3 s into the light activation (Figure 3H, magenta trace and Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: This is a result from optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claims.claim: PDM-DN>CsChrimson larvae spent significantly more time sweeping their head throughout the light flash compared to parental controls.

results.result: A loss-of-function screen using ~300 Split-Gal4 driver lines with tetanus toxin light chain silencing identified 18 lines with significant chemotaxis defects, including a line specifically labeling the olfactory descending neuron PDM-DN that connects the lateral horn to the ventral nerve cord.
results.evaluation: The screen methodology is well-described (C31-C39), with appropriate controls and quantification. The identification of PDM-DN (C41) is supported by anatomical data in Figures 1C and 2A. The screen design using multiple odor sources to minimize larval interactions (C38) and the use of high-throughput tracking (C33) are methodologically sound. Sample size of ~300 lines (C39) is adequate for discovery.

results.result: Silencing PDM-DN reduced chemotaxis accuracy, with larvae remaining ~19 mm from odor sources (vs. ~13 mm for controls) during 120-240s, due to decreased turn rate rather than reduced locomotor speed, though residual chemotaxis ability remained.
results.evaluation: The behavioral phenotype is quantitatively characterized with appropriate controls (C42-C44, Figure 1D-F). The dissociation between turn rate defect (C46) and normal locomotor speed (C45) is demonstrated with proper statistical analysis. The incomplete phenotype (C47) is consistent with redundant pathways. However, genetic background effects between parental controls (C64) introduce some uncertainty about the magnitude of effects.

results.result: PDM-DN consists of bilaterally symmetrical neurons with somas in the posterior-dorsal-medial brain region, dendrites around the mushroom body peduncle and lateral horn, and axons projecting contralaterally to the SEZ, thoracic neuromeres, and first four abdominal segments.
results.evaluation: The anatomical characterization is thorough, using both light microscopy (C48-C52, Figure 2A) and MCFO technique (C49, Figure 2Aiv). The identification in EM based on morphological matching (C53, Figure 2B) is well-justified. The dendritic localization near olfactory processing centers (C51) provides anatomical support for functional role.

results.result: EM reconstruction revealed that PDM-DN receives olfactory input from Or42a and Or42b OSNs via a feedforward circuit motif involving lateral horn interneurons LH-LN1 and LH-LN2.
results.evaluation: The circuit reconstruction is supported by EM data (C55-C58, Figure 2C and supplements). The connection to Or42a/Or42b is consistent with the behavioral screen using ethyl butyrate (C54). The feedforward motif identification (C59) is appropriately referenced to circuit theory. However, the signs of interactions remain unknown, limiting mechanistic interpretation.

results.result: In single-larva tracking assays, PDM-DN silencing specifically impaired turn initiation during down-gradient runs (not up-gradient runs), without affecting locomotor speed or turn accuracy, and had no effect in the absence of odor gradients.
results.evaluation: The single-larva tracking provides higher resolution than group assays (C60-C62, Figure 3A-C). The dissociation between down-gradient and up-gradient effects (C66-C68) is a key finding supported by appropriate conditioning of the analysis. Controls without odor (C69) rule out general motor defects. However, genetic background differences between controls (C64) remain a concern.

results.result: PDM-DN silencing did not affect turn orientation accuracy, though one parental control showed reduced turning performance possibly due to speed-accuracy tradeoffs.
results.evaluation: The dissociation between turn timing and turn direction (C70) is an important finding suggesting separate pathways. The observation about one parental control (C71-C72) is appropriately interpreted as a potential speed-accuracy tradeoff, though this remains speculative. This result supports the specificity of PDM-DN function.

results.result: Optogenetic activation of PDM-DN produced highly reproducible, deterministic stops (probability near 1.0 vs. near 0 for controls) independent of tail speed, with stereotyped decreases in tail speed averaging over 280 trials.
results.evaluation: The optogenetic experiments demonstrate robust, reproducible effects (C73-C76, Figure 3E-F, Video 1). The deterministic nature is well-characterized through probability analysis (C79, C81) and independence from tail speed (C81). Controls show only modest startle responses (C78, C80). The large sample size (280 flashes, C76) provides strong statistical power. Inter-trial variability is appropriately acknowledged (C77).

results.result: During prolonged 20-s optogenetic activation, PDM-DN-induced stopping behavior was sustained for only ~3s before tail speed gradually increased, suggesting neuronal adaptation or circuit-level bypass mechanisms.
results.evaluation: The temporal dynamics of prolonged activation are clearly documented (C82, Figure 3—figure supplement 3A). The interpretation of adaptation or bypass mechanisms (C83) is reasonable given the data, though the specific mechanism cannot be determined from these experiments. This result provides important constraints on PDM-DN function.

results.result: PDM-DN activation induced delayed head-casting behavior (peaking at ~3s) that varied strongly across trials and showed sensitivity to sensory experience, suggesting less direct control than stopping behavior.
results.evaluation: The head-casting phenotype is well-characterized (C84-C85, Figure 3H-I) with appropriate comparison to controls. The high inter-trial variability (C86) and sensory dependence (C87, Figure 3—figure supplement 5) support the interpretation of indirect control. This contrasts appropriately with the stereotyped stopping behavior.

results.result: Unilateral PDM-DN activation was sufficient to induce stopping and head-casting, and PDM-DN activation prolonged ongoing stops (4.66±0.35s vs. 2.81±0.11s for controls), indicating state-independent function.
results.evaluation: The unilateral activation experiment (C88) demonstrates that bilateral activation is not required. The state-independence is supported by experiments during head-casting (C89-C90, Figure 3—figure supplement 3C-D). The quantitative comparison of stop durations provides clear evidence. The conclusion about state-independence (C91) is well-supported.

results.result: In odor gradients, PDM-DN activation induced stopping independent of gradient direction, but head-casting showed remarkable sensitivity to sensory experience, being more vigorous during down-gradient runs than up-gradient runs.
results.evaluation: The experiments in odor gradients (C92-C95, Figure 3J-M) demonstrate differential effects on stopping vs. head-casting. The sensory-dependent modulation of head-casting (C93-C95) is well-documented. Controls show startle responses override olfactory information (C96). The summary conclusion (C97) appropriately integrates these findings. This supports a hierarchical organization of motor outputs.

results.result: Forward locomotion consists of wave-like peristaltic contractions from posterior to anterior segments, with the wave cycle defined as the period between peak tail speed and subsequent peak body length, described as phases from 0-360 degrees.
results.evaluation: These claims establish the framework for analyzing peristalsis (C98-C102, Figure 4A). The definitions are based on well-established principles (C98-C99 cite Heckscher et al., 2012) and are clearly operationalized for the current study (C100-C102). This provides necessary context for subsequent mechanistic analysis.

results.result: PDM-DN activation caused steep decreases in tail speed (~1s after flash onset) regardless of wave phase, while body length continued increasing to maximum, with larvae remaining fully extended before relaxing, indicating that PDM-DN allows ongoing wave completion but suppresses subsequent wave initiation.
results.evaluation: The phase-independent effects on tail speed (C103-C104, Figure 4B) and body length (C105-C106, Figure 4C) are well-documented across different phases. The interpretation that PDM-DN allows wave completion but blocks initiation (C107) is a logical inference from the kinematic data. This is a key mechanistic insight.

results.result: Tracking segmental contractions revealed that PDM-DN activation during late wave phases (A1-A3) allowed wave completion, but activation during early phases (A7) or at the hinge point (A4) could terminate waves prematurely, with segment A4 representing a critical hinge point beyond which waves cannot be terminated.
results.evaluation: The segmental analysis (C108-C111, Figure 4E) provides detailed spatial resolution of PDM-DN effects. The identification of A4 as a hinge point (C112) is supported by multiple observations. However, some variability is noted (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), suggesting the effect is not absolute. The conclusion is well-supported but acknowledges complexity.

results.result: In isolated CNS preparations showing fictive locomotion, PDM-DN activation terminated waves at the hinge point (A4) and severely suppressed subsequent wave initiation, with wave frequency ~5-10x slower than intact larvae, demonstrating that PDM-DN inhibits wave initiation in posterior segments independent of sensory feedback.
results.evaluation: The fictive locomotion experiments (C113-C119, Figure 4G-H) provide strong evidence that PDM-DN effects are intrinsic to the CNS. The wave termination at A4 (C117) is consistent with intact larva experiments. The reduced wave frequency (C116) is appropriately noted and consistent with prior work. The conclusion about posterior segment inhibition (C120) integrates multiple lines of evidence.

results.result: The A27h network of segmentally repeated excitatory premotor neurons, which excites motor neurons and inhibitory GDL neurons to propagate forward waves, is hypothesized to be the target of PDM-DN action based on the deterministic stopping phenotype.
results.evaluation: The description of the A27h network (C121-C125) is well-supported by citations to prior work. The hypothesis that PDM-DN acts on A27h (C126) is a reasonable inference from the behavioral phenotype and known circuit organization. This sets up the subsequent EM reconstruction experiments.

results.result: EM reconstruction revealed that PDM-DN connects to the A27h premotor network through the descending neuron SEZ-DN1, which has dendritic arbors in the SEZ and exclusively targets A27h neurons in posterior segments (A5-A7), with no connections anterior to the hinge point A4.
results.evaluation: The EM reconstruction (C127-C131, Figure 5 and supplements) provides detailed anatomical evidence for the PDM-DN to A27h pathway via SEZ-DN1. The restriction of SEZ-DN1 connections to posterior segments (C130-C131) is consistent with the functional data showing A4 as a hinge point. The identification of a specific driver line (C132) enables functional validation.

results.result: Immunostaining showed PDM-DN co-localizes with choline acetyltransferase but not GABA or glutamate, and RNAi knockdown of ChAT abolished the PDM-DN gain-of-function phenotype, demonstrating that PDM-DN is cholinergic and acetylcholine release is necessary for PDM-DN-evoked pauses.
results.evaluation: The neurotransmitter profiling (C133-C134, Figure 5B and supplement) uses appropriate immunostaining methods. The RNAi experiment (C135-C136, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) provides functional validation that acetylcholine is necessary. This is strong evidence for the cholinergic identity of PDM-DN.

results.result: SEZ-DN1 co-localizes with GABA immunostaining and optogenetic activation produces stop/cast transitions similar to PDM-DN, demonstrating that SEZ-DN1 is a GABAergic inhibitory neuron that acts on the A27h network in posterior segments.
results.evaluation: The GABA immunostaining (C138, Figure 5C) and optogenetic validation (C139, Figure 5D-E, Video 3) provide converging evidence for SEZ-DN1 function. The logical inference that SEZ-DN1 must be inhibitory (C137) is supported by the circuit logic. The conclusion (C140) appropriately integrates anatomical and functional data.

results.result: PDM-DN employs distinct SEZ and abdominal interneurons to differentially regulate stopping and head-casting behaviors, with bilateral PDM-DN input to SEZ-DN1 in segments A6-A7, and absence of connectivity anterior to A4 corroborated by functional data.
results.evaluation: The summary conclusion (C141) is supported by the detailed anatomical (C142) and functional (C143) data. The integration of EM connectivity with functional observations provides strong support for differential regulation of behavioral modules. This is a key organizational principle of the circuit.

results.result: PDM-DN has two additional SEZ partners: SEZ-LN1, which connects asymmetrically to RP motor neurons controlling dorsal/ventral muscles (potentially contributing to head sweeps), and SEZ-DN2, which innervates premotor neurons upstream of PaN motor neurons (possibly contributing to head-scanning behavior).
results.evaluation: The anatomical connections are documented by EM (C144-C146, C148-C149, Figure 5—figure supplement 2), but functional validation is lacking due to absence of specific driver lines. The proposed roles in head-casting (C147, C150) are speculative. While the anatomy is solid, the functional significance remains uncertain without experimental validation.

results.result: Optogenetic activation of SEZ-DN1 blocked forward wave propagation when waves were posterior to the hinge point (A4) and suppressed fictive locomotion waves in isolated CNS, with drastically reduced wave numbers during light flashes.
results.evaluation: The SEZ-DN1 optogenetic experiments (C151-C154, Figure 6A-D) parallel the PDM-DN experiments and provide strong functional validation of the pathway. The effects on both intact larvae (C151-C152) and fictive locomotion (C153-C154) demonstrate that SEZ-DN1 is sufficient to block wave initiation. This validates the proposed circuit mechanism.

results.result: Calcium imaging demonstrated that PDM-DN activation excited neural activity in SEZ-DN1 axons, validating a model where PDM-DN activates SEZ-DN1, which in turn inhibits the A27h premotor system.
results.evaluation: The calcium imaging experiments (C155-C156, Figure 6E-F) provide direct functional evidence for excitatory transmission from PDM-DN to SEZ-DN1. The validation of the circuit model (C157) integrates multiple lines of evidence (EM, neurotransmitter profiling, optogenetics, calcium imaging). This is strong support for the proposed mechanism.

results.result: Larval chemotaxis, like bacterial and C. elegans chemotaxis, uses a conserved algorithm where positive gradients extend runs and negative gradients promote stops and turns, implemented through four behavioral primitives: runs, stops, head casts, and turns.
results.evaluation: These claims establish the behavioral and evolutionary context (C1, C5-C12). They are well-supported by citations to prior work and represent established knowledge in the field. This provides the necessary background for understanding the significance of the circuit mechanisms identified in this study.

results.result: Prior optogenetic studies established quantitative relationships between OSN activity and motor programs, and the larval olfactory system anatomy (21 OSNs projecting to PNs in the antennal lobe, then to lateral horn and mushroom body) has been characterized by light and electron microscopy.
results.evaluation: These claims summarize prior work on the larval olfactory system (C13-C21) and are appropriately supported by citations. They establish the state of knowledge before the current study and justify the focus on descending pathways as the missing link between sensory processing and motor control.

results.result: Premotor circuits in the VNC generate peristaltic motion through CPG networks, and descending neurons create a bottleneck in sensorimotor transformations, with examples from leech and adult Drosophila showing that most descending neurons produce single behavioral outputs.
results.evaluation: These claims establish the conceptual framework for understanding descending neuron function (C22-C30) and are well-supported by citations to prior work. They provide important context for interpreting the PDM-DN results in the broader context of command-like neurons across species.
